date_label: Fellow prisoners in Reading; the recommendation is of June 1897
summary: Lawley - or possibly Langley; the editors of Wilde's letters could not settle it - was a soldier who served time in Reading with Wilde and struck him as quiet and well conducted. In a postscript to a long, raw letter written a month after his release, Wilde put in a word to get him a place as a groom. That postscript is the whole of him.

sources.quote: With regard to Lawley. All soldiers are neat, and smart, and make capital servants. He would be a good groom; he is, I believe, a Third Hussars man. He was a quiet well-conducted chap in Reading always.
sources.context: A postscript, printed in italic beneath Wilde's signature, to a long letter of June 1897 whose main body is about a brother prisoner released on 4 June and about the writer's own hurt feelings. The editors' footnote to the name reads, in full, "Or possibly Langley." Wilde signs the letter itself "your sincere friend and admirer".
sources.supports: That the man existed, that Wilde thought well of him, and how little else the record kept.
sources.provenance: PDF p. 947 read as a rendered page image; printed folio 897 confirmed at the foot of the image. Located first in the complete OCR mirror, which locates only. Superscript note markers omitted as typography.
